title: Coalition takes aim at business regulators' war on risk
full_text:
The Coalition wants to force Australia's financial regulators to do more to promote competition and industry growth, arguing their focus on minimising risk is stifling innovation.
Shadow treasurer Tim Wilson on Tuesday will call for an "attitudinal reset" at the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority and Australian Securities and Investments Commission, following criticism from industry and economists that financial sector regulation is stymying growth.
The Coalition has long had a frosty relationship with financial regulators. Opposition housing spokesman Andrew Bragg has regularly argued that APRA's requirement for banks to test borrowers' ability to withstand a 3 percentage point rise in interest rates locks prospective first-home buyers out of the market.
"Currently regulators are tasked with minimising risk. The incentive for regulators is to impose more complex regulation and costs on businesses. They lack an obligation to weigh decisions against the consequences of market entry and industry growth," Wilson will tell a conference hosted by the Australian Finance Industry Association, according to a copy of his speaking notes.
"That needs to change. Regulators fulfil an important function in our economy, but it must be weighed against the consequences of their decisions."
Former Treasury secretary Martin Parkinson last year warned that aggressive corporate regulators were hurting the economy with a "gotcha" approach against business and their administrative red tape was stifling investment.
He said corporate regulators had usurped their remit by trying to become policymakers, adding that politicians and bureaucrats in Canberra had no idea how ASIC and the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission were smothering business with red tape.
Wilson says in his speech that he is interested in adopting the Monetary Authority of Singapore's dual mandate, where it balances its role as a regulator with the need to encourage the finance industry to flourish. A mandate to weigh decisions against industry growth promotes "internal tension" so regulators understand the consequences of their decisions, Wilson says.
The trade-off for having a higher risk tolerance would be that penalties for non-compliance by large operators would need to be heavier.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers in July released new statements of expectations for APRA and ASIC, telling the regulators they should support growth by taking a proportionate, risk-based approach to regulation.
The move followed last year's Economic Reform Roundtable, which heard that excessive regulation was reducing productivity.
Ahead of the roundtable, the Productivity Commission warned that red tape was out of control and recommended a suite of proposals to overhaul regulations it said were strangling the economy. In one instance, now widely cited by the business community, the PC found that to open a cafe in Brisbane the owner would have to engage in 31 regulatory steps before they could "even contemplate charging $5.50 for a flat white".
"Regulators and policymakers ... can face incentives to be overly risk-averse, to underweight the burden that regulations place on businesses, and to pursue narrow goals at the expense of broader economy-wide goals," the PC said in an interim report on creating a more dynamic and resilient economy.
